extracted.intended_audience: educators, instructional designers, and distance-learning practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the affordances, limitations, and pedagogical uses of various online learning technologies (e.g., IM, PDAs, wikis, virtual worlds, learning objects) and general characteristics that determine their appropriateness for distance education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instant messaging suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength lies in its ability to facilitate immediate contact with other students and teachers, or with a tutor who is supervising chat sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instant messaging is highly transportable (usable on multiple devices), offers immediate and delayed message delivery, and increased functionality via central servers; however, it has not yet been used as an efficient content-delivery teaching tool and is best used for immediate contact, tutoring, and facilitation of synchronous interaction rather than long-form content delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-held and wireless device affordances
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-held devices are very powerful small computers offering web browsers, instant messaging, email, multimedia capabilities, and a previously unknown degree of flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As affordable high-bandwidth access increases and wireless device costs drop, these devices can enable near-universal access, potentially reduce reliance on paper/textbooks, and deliver graphics and video anywhere. Consider device form factors (phones, tablets, e-books), multimedia capability, interoperability, bandwidth needs, and the readiness of course materials for small-screen/mobile use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-to-peer (P2P) educational potential
rubrics_metrics.description: P2P applications allow users to share files directly between users and can be used to offer research and other materials online to be 'harvested' by well-designed P2P programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P2P can enable wide distribution and sharing of learning objects and resources; structured metadata on P2P systems can enhance community activities and information structuring. Be mindful of legal/ethical issues (e.g., copyright controversies) and design P2P systems to support educational metadata and discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blog use for learning and knowledge sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Blogs (weblogs) serve as personal journals or newsletters and can be used for knowledge sharing, networking, course announcements, student submissions, journals, and e-portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blogs are generally easy to create and can host text, audio, and video (vlogs). They support commenting and community interaction, reflective writing, real-world digital knowledge management, group work, and linking to external professionals. Use blogs for assignments, announcements, annotated reading links, and student portfolios, while attending to moderation and assessment practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: RSS/Atom for timely content aggregation and personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: RSS (and Atom) support distribution of content and enable personalization by allowing a user's device to fetch information of interest as it becomes available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RSS aggregators permit timely sharing of updates (news, podcasts, videocasts) and facilitate educators' access to updated teaching content from multiple sources. Use RSS to support teacher-to-teacher sharing, student social networks with peer-produced content, and aggregation of multimedia resources; consider interoperability issues across feed formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wikis for collaborative authoring and course resources
rubrics_metrics.description: A wiki is a collection of web pages where users can insert and edit content collectively and is useful for posting course information, lecture notes, and inviting student participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikis enable co-construction of knowledge, simple hyperlinking and markup, open or closed access models, and can serve as student/group project sites, e-portfolios, brainstorming spaces, and FAQ pages. They require community maintenance and attention to versioning, authorship, and assessment of contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual worlds for simulation and experiential learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual worlds are simulated environments accessed online where users interact via avatars and can engage in real-time communication, simulations, role-playing, and experiential learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use virtual worlds to create flexible, imaginative learning spaces for safe practice, computer-based simulations, and global collaboration. They support VoIP/live video and can host massive multiplayer experiences; consider design for pedagogical objectives, logistical complexity, access, and potential for authentic practice without real-world consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital games as reinforcement and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational games reinforce learning by offering immediate feedback and recurring gratification, prolonging learner interest and motivating learners by making learning enjoyable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games can support diverse learner types, provide immediate feedback, and help maintain engagement while reinforcing concepts introduced via other methods. Choose game types (puzzlers, role-playing, strategy) that align with learning objectives, and use games primarily to reinforce rather than replace core instruction unless explicitly designed otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objects: reusability and standards-based interoperability
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning objects are discrete lessons or units (text, audio, video, interactive files) whose principal benefit comes from reusability and standards-based structure enabling use across LMSs and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning objects with metadata and interoperability standards so they can be harvested, reused, and integrated into many courses. Evidence suggests objects-based courses can improve efficiency (e.g., reduced time to complete tasks). Consider metadata quality, repository design, and pedagogical context to maximize reuse and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media as tools for cooperation, collaboration, and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning media are tools for cooperation, collaboration, and communication and allow provision of teaching presence, structure, learning and technology support, orientation to new roles and processes, and interaction with the tutor and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a medium, consider how it supports coordination, cooperative tasks, and co-construction of knowledge; also evaluate the degree to which it enables teaching presence, scaffolding, orientation to processes, and ongoing interaction between learners and instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No medium is universally appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: No medium, however technologically elegant, is de facto appropriate for all student audiences or learning contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match media choice to learner characteristics, context, and learning objectives. Practitioners should understand affordances and limitations, monitor technological trends, and avoid assuming a single technology fits all needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of course design and pedagogy over media
rubrics_metrics.description: Course design and pedagogy are always more important than media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on technology alone to transform learning; solid pedagogical design should drive media selection and use. Review prior research and pedagogical principles rather than adopting tools solely for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust interaction to individual learner needs
rubrics_metrics.description: All interaction is not equally useful; interaction should be adjusted to individual needs and preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online learners perceive transactional distance differently and require varying forms and amounts of interaction and instructor support. Design interaction types and frequency to align with learner preferences, support levels, and communication styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations of learner autonomy and control
rubrics_metrics.description: Online learning designs usually expect the learner to exercise more autonomy and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some learners (e.g., field-dependent or less mature undergraduates) may struggle with high autonomy and may need extra structure, scaffolding, or instructor watchfulness. Align expectations about learner self-regulation with learner readiness and provide supports where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of structure in online environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure in the learning environment is usually plentiful in face-to-face situations and potentially essential online where sound study skills or habits may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear organization, schedules, milestones, and scaffolds in online courses—especially for less mature learners. Instructor presence that is 'watchful and helpful' can mitigate reduced structure and improve outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media support community-building through structured interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive media support communities, based on what people do together, not where or when; community becomes a process in which 'structured and systematic' social interaction is essential to significant learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that create shared goals and structured interaction to foster learning communities. Use media to facilitate ongoing, purposeful collaboration rather than episodic or purely social contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled instructor use required
rubrics_metrics.description: Responding to individual online learning preferences requires skilled uses of media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors must be able to select, configure, and adapt media to suit learner needs and pedagogical aims. Professional development and monitoring of media effectiveness are necessary to align tools with learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance advantages and disadvantages of media
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages (flexibility, reuse, improved literacy, alleviating overcrowding, expanded access) are counterbalanced by disadvantages (quality concerns, fair treatment of distance faculty, employer skepticism, reduced spontaneous interaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a balanced assessment when choosing and implementing media. Consider institutional, pedagogical, quality-assurance, staffing, and social impacts as well as potential benefits when introducing technologies.
